routes.description: Establish that people sometimes face genuinely available alternatives, exercise control over which alternative occurs, and thereby possess the kind of freedom capable of grounding responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by supporting alternatives and agent control, answering the inference from pervasive causal influence to exhaustive determination, and connecting that freedom to deliberation, normative requirements, and desert-sensitive responsibility.

motionBridge.description: Show that genuine alternatives and control sometimes exist and can justify responsibility for the action selected.

centralBridges.description: Explain why causal influence, probabilistic pressure, and reason-giving explanation need not eliminate every genuinely available alternative.
Supply a defensible basis for believing in freedom while addressing challenges to intuition, appearances, deliberation, and reason-responsive belief.
Show why responsibility and normative practices require feasible alternatives or desert beyond purely forward-looking behavioral management.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Clarify the incompatibilist and possible compatibilist concepts at stake when control, fixed history, and the ability to do otherwise are compared.
Explain how reasons can make free action intelligible even if the final selection is not determined by a further cause.

routes.description: Establish that behavior remains within an integrated chain of biological and environmental causes, leaving no agent-controlled selection among genuinely available alternatives and no desert-based responsibility.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds by connecting multi-timescale causal explanation to the exclusion of libertarian control, rebutting intuition-based and practical objections, and deriving responsibility practices that do not depend on retribution or earned moral entitlement.

motionBridge.description: Show that antecedent causation excludes genuine alternative control and therefore cannot justify desert-based responsibility.

centralBridges.description: Integrate immediate, neural, physiological, developmental, genetic, cultural, and historical causes into a continuous account of behavior.
Explain why expanding mechanistic evidence and the absence of causally independent action undermine reliance on experienced freedom.
Show how learning, intervention, deliberative inputs, and behavioral change can operate causally without agent-originating freedom.
Connect causal explanation to rejection of retribution and differential desert while preserving forward-looking social responses.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Distinguish agent control from randomness so that indeterminacy does not itself establish freely authored choice.
Account for gratitude and other responsibility-adjacent practices through evolutionary and mechanistic functions without presupposing free choice.

sections.title: Causal explanation, influence, and genuinely available alternatives
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether the integrated biological and environmental causal account exhausts the explanation of conduct or merely influences choices while leaving some alternatives available.

sections.title: Intuition, scientific evidence, and the burden of proof
sections.rationale: This issue determines whether experienced freedom and intellectual appearances supply a rational default, or whether mechanistic discoveries and historical error require withholding or revising that belief.

sections.title: Control, deliberation, change, and reason-responsive agency
sections.rationale: This issue addresses whether deliberation, advice, belief formation, learning, and reasons can constitute meaningful control or remain fully intelligible as determined causal processes.

sections.title: Responsibility, moral desert, punishment, and humane practice
sections.rationale: This issue connects the metaphysical dispute to the motion's responsibility clause by testing retribution, innocence, entitlement, blame, and forward-looking approaches to harmful behavior.

sections.title: Concepts of freedom, explanatory stopping points, and indeterminacy
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies incompatibilist and compatibilist definitions, whether choice can terminate explanation at an agent's reasons, and why randomness alone may fail to provide agency.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Behavioral choices arise from causal influences extending from immediate cues and physiology through development, genes, culture, and deep history.
moves.attributionBasis: This uninterrupted opening-statement sequence remains in Sapolsky's voice and develops the empirical case he announced at the outset.

response.rationale: This constructive move supplies the empirical foundation of the con causal-chain route and therefore has no earlier opposing target.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it develops a broad and concrete multiscale causal foundation.

precisionFindings.rationale: The causal-influence proposition and its several timescales are recoverable, with exhaustive significance left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples strongly support pervasive influence, while the move itself stops short of making the later exhaustive inference.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The timescale progression is internally consistent, though its integration remains partly compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Specific physiological, developmental, genetic, and cultural examples provide substantial representative support.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supplies the indispensable multiscale content of the con causal-chain bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The constructive catalog does not engage a sufficiently developed opposing alternative for a charity test.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt specifically invokes childhood adversity and ACE scores within a longer progression across immediate and historical antecedents.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Biological and environmental influences form a seamless causal arc that leaves no explanatory gap in which freely controlled alternatives operate.
moves.attributionBasis: Sapolsky explicitly synthesizes his preceding examples and closes his opening statement before the moderator resumes control.

response.rationale: This constructive synthesis advances the con motion route by inferring that the integrated causal arc leaves no room for free will.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it clearly states the central synthesis but compresses its decisive exclusion inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The conclusion is clear, but “no room” shifts from comprehensive influence to exclusion without an explicit control criterion.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical exclusion of free will outruns the supplied evidence of pervasive biological and environmental influence.

logicalCoherence.rationale: A material bridge from continuous causal influence to the impossibility of agent-controlled alternatives is missing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The preceding causal examples support influence but do not independently verify exhaustive determination or exclusion.

relevanceBurden.rationale: The stated no-room conclusion directly advances the con motion-level completion condition.

representationalCharity.rationale: This synthesis asserts its own conclusion without developing an opposing interpretation sufficiently to test charity.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly describes a seamless biological-environmental arc and concludes that it leaves no room for free will whatsoever.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Free will consists in sometimes having multiple possibilities available and exercising control over which of those possibilities is realized.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator introduces Huemer's opening statement, and Huemer explicitly presents his understanding of the disputed thesis and its implications.

response.rationale: This constructive move defines the pro motion thesis as genuine alternatives plus control over which alternative is realized.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it gives a clear motion-level conception but offers little independent support for its existence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move explicitly limits its claim to sometimes and clearly identifies alternatives, control, and realization.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As an announced definition of the thesis rather than proof of its truth, the force fits the supporting content.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The definition is consistent and explicit, with only the deeper analysis of control left undeveloped.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The passage clearly establishes the proposed concept but supplies limited evidence that actual choices instantiate it.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It states the alternatives-and-control content at the heart of the pro motion bridge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move primarily states its own conception and does not yet assess a developed opposing alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says that more than one action can be available and that it is up to the person which is realized.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Deliberation, advice, evaluation, reward, and retributive punishment would not make sense if people never had alternatives available to them.
moves.attributionBasis: The passage is a continuous part of Huemer's prepared opening and uses his stated hard-determinist framework throughout.

response.rationale: This constructive move argues from deliberation, advice, reward, and punishment practices to the need for available alternatives.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it identifies several consequential practices but compresses the presupposition-to-truth inference.

precisionFindings.rationale: The practical claim is clear, though the intended sense of “make sense” and its exceptions remain implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical practical conclusions are stronger than the argument establishing that no forward-looking reinterpretation is possible.

charity.alternative: Deliberation, advice, reward, and punishment can function as causal and forward-looking practices under determinism.
charity.decisiveQualification: Functional usefulness would not by itself preserve retributive desert or genuinely available alternatives.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument leaves a material bridge from practices presupposing alternatives to alternatives actually existing.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Familiar practices illustrate the claim, but no comparison with causal or forward-looking accounts is developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the pro central responsibility bridge through deliberation and desert-sensitive practices.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move groups diverse practices together and does not fully address their strongest deterministic functional interpretation.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt expressly says deliberation presupposes alternatives and extends the contention to advice, reward, and retributive punishment.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Arguing for or rationally accepting determinism is self-defeating because argument and rational belief invoke reasons, while reasons to act require that the action be both possible and avoidable.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer labels and develops the self-defeat portion of his opening, distinguishes prior formulations, and then presents his own connected arguments.

response.rationale: This constructive move argues that determinist advocacy undermines the reasons and rational belief on which that advocacy depends.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: Within constructive moves, it presents an explicit self-defeat structure but relies on a controversial premise about reasons.

precisionFindings.rationale: The inference is recoverable, but “reason” moves between reasons for action and reasons for belief without defense.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The universal conclusion that determinism eliminates all reasons exceeds the support for its avoidability premise.

charity.alternative: Reasons may causally explain and rationally support beliefs even when the resulting belief is determined.
charity.decisiveQualification: A causal explanation of belief does not alone show that the belief lacks epistemic warrant.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-defeat conclusion depends on an unsupported transfer from avoidable action to rationally supported belief.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The central premise that unavoidable actions or beliefs cannot have reasons is asserted rather than independently defended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the pro central epistemic bridge by challenging the rational status of determinism.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move does not engage the strongest deterministic distinction between causal production and rational support.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt explicitly claims arguments supply reasons, determinism eliminates reasons, and therefore any argument for determinism defeats itself.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: The felt obviousness of freely choosing is not reliable evidence because compelling intuitive explanations have repeatedly yielded to mechanistic accounts.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator assigns Sapolsky the rebuttal, and he explicitly identifies Huemer's reliance on intuition before supplying counterexamples.

components.text: Whether the rational case for determinism can survive Huemer’s appeal to reasons and intellectual appearances.
Whether the apparent obviousness of freely selecting among alternatives is trustworthy evidence.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the epistemic reliance underlying Huemer’s case by arguing that compelling intuitions have repeatedly yielded to mechanistic explanation, but it does not directly solve the reasons-based self-defeat inference.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a partial answer that contacts the decisive epistemic component while leaving the distinct self-defeat structure unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: The skeptical induction is clear, though intuition, appearance, and folk causal explanation are treated somewhat interchangeably.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Historical errors warrant caution, but do not alone establish that the specific experience of agency is unreliable.

charity.alternative: The free-will appearance may be a direct seeming rather than a historical folk theory inferred from sparse observations.
charity.decisiveQualification: Past intuitive error lowers generic trust without showing that every class of appearance is equally unreliable.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The skeptical induction is coherent, but the analogy to experienced agency requires a material similarity premise.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Multiple historical examples support fallibility, while representativeness for free-will experience remains compressed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the pro central epistemic case by challenging reliance on intuitive obviousness.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply uses vivid analogies but does not distinguish the strongest direct-appearance version of the opposing case.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt invokes the witch explanation for hailstorms as one example in a historical argument for suspicion toward intuition.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Determinism permits behavioral change because learning and changed conditions mechanistically alter organisms and their subsequent responses.
moves.attributionBasis: This remains within Sapolsky's designated rebuttal and explicitly addresses an implication he attributes to critics of hard incompatibilism.

components.text: Whether advice, learning, and behavioral change remain intelligible if people lack freely available alternatives.
Whether rational or behavioral change requires an agent’s avoidable selection rather than causal alteration.

response.rationale: The reply directly explains change as mechanistic conditioning and altered inputs, contacting the practical intelligibility objection while not fully addressing retribution or epistemic normativity.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a strong partial answer that reaches the decisive change component but not every practice bundled into the target.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between choosing to change and being changed by mechanisms is clearly and consistently stated.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Conditioning and altered conditions adequately support the bounded claim that deterministic systems can change.

charity.alternative: Advice and deliberation may be exercises of agent control rather than merely external mechanisms producing change.
charity.decisiveQualification: Showing causal contribution does not by itself establish exhaustive determination, though it answers the claim that change is impossible.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between change and self-originating choice is clear and directly resolves the alleged incompatibility.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Conditioning examples substantiate mechanistic change, with the extrapolation to complex deliberation only partly developed.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central practical-compatibility bridge through a causal account of learning and change.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly preserves the practical objection’s force while giving a substantive causal account of change.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt contrasts choosing to change with being changed and cites conditioned responses and altered perceptions as mechanisms.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Examples of biological or environmental influence do not establish complete determination, and cases involving impairment do not eliminate freedom in ordinary, unimpaired decisions.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator gives Huemer the rebuttal, and Huemer expressly identifies examples from Sapolsky's opening before challenging their inferential force.

components.text: Whether examples of pervasive biological and environmental influence establish exhaustive determination and eliminate alternatives.
Whether impaired or abnormal cases can establish the absence of freedom in ordinary unimpaired choices.

response.rationale: The reply expressly identifies two inferential defects: influence is not determination, and impaired cases do not automatically generalize to ordinary cases; those defects undercut the con synthesis if sustained.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies the decisive inference and generalization failures and states their defeating consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: Influence, complete determination, impaired cases, and ordinary cases are distinctly and consistently compared.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The negative claim that the cited examples do not entail exhaustive determination fits the logical evidence offered.

charity.alternative: The con examples are intended as representative pieces of a cumulative causal account, not merely isolated pathologies.
charity.decisiveQualification: Even a cumulative influence account still needs a bridge showing that no agent-controlled alternative remains.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The distinction between influence and determination supplies a clear and valid diagnostic challenge to the con inference.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The impairment contrast supports the generalization objection, though the prevalence of allegedly abnormal examples is not documented.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the indispensable causal-chain inference from antecedent influences to exhaustive determination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply recognizes cumulative influence yet accurately preserves the unresolved inference to exhaustive determination.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt labels an inference from bad cases to good cases and distinguishes psychiatric or impaired examples from ordinary decisions.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Intellectual appearances are indispensable sources of justification, and challenges to free will themselves rely on intuitive and logical appearances.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer announces a response to Sapolsky's discussion of intuition and continues that epistemological reply through the final delivered context row.

components.text: Whether historical intuitive errors defeat the justificatory role of present intellectual appearances concerning free will.
Whether the con argument can reject appearances without itself relying on logical and intellectual appearances.

response.rationale: The reply attacks the skeptical demand by arguing that appearances are indispensable to justification and that the con reasoning itself relies on them, although it does not establish equal reliability across kinds of appearance.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly identifies a self-applicative defect in wholesale intuition skepticism and states the epistemic consequence.

precisionFindings.rationale: The justificatory thesis is clear, but intuition and intellectual appearance are distinguished only partially.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Some reliance on appearances may be indispensable without every specific appearance having equal prima facie weight.

charity.alternative: The con position can distrust a particular class of agency intuitions without rejecting all appearances or logical seemings.
charity.decisiveQualification: Selective skepticism needs a principled reliability distinction rather than a wholesale historical analogy.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The self-application point is strong, though indispensability does not fully establish the targeted appearance’s reliability.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The argument is primarily epistemic and internally supported, with limited comparison among different appearance types.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the pro central epistemic bridge against the con challenge to intuition.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply exposes overbroad skepticism but somewhat compresses the strongest selective-skeptic alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt defines intuition as a kind of appearance and begins the claim that justification ultimately depends on appearances.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Practical difficulty imagining life without free-will-based praise and blame does not make retribution or differential moral entitlement justified.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly gives Sapolsky the floor, and the continuous turn states his mechanistic orientation and consequences for punishment.

components.text: Whether praise, blame, reward, and punishment must retain their free-will-based and retributive forms to remain intelligible.
Whether agent-controlled alternatives justify differential moral entitlement and retribution.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the responsibility demand by rejecting the inference from practical difficulty to moral justification, though it concedes uncertainty about implementation and does not yet supply a full replacement practice.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It contacts the decisive moral-justification component but only partially answers the practical-function component.

precisionFindings.rationale: The move clearly separates difficulty of social functioning from justification of retribution and differential entitlement.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker expressly acknowledges practical uncertainty, though the claim of superior moral alignment remains underargued.

charity.alternative: Responsibility practices may encode desert while also serving coordination, deterrence, and moral communication.
charity.decisiveQualification: Practical utility alone does not establish that differential suffering is deserved.

logicalCoherence.rationale: It validly separates feasibility anxiety from moral justification, while its positive moral standard remains compressed.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The rejection of retribution relies mainly on assertion about moral alignment rather than a developed normative warrant.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central responsibility-revision bridge by rejecting retribution and entitlement.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply fairly distinguishes utility from desert and does not reduce the opposing concern to mere social panic.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt acknowledges uncertainty about functioning without praise and blame while denying that difficulty justifies retribution.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Deterrence and incapacitation alone cannot explain why framing an innocent ex-convict is wrong while imposing the same punishment on the actual offender is permissible.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn begins with Huemer answering Sapolsky's punishment claim and develops one continuous framing thought experiment to its stated intuitive conclusion.

components.text: Whether purely forward-looking deterrence can distinguish permissible punishment of an offender from framing an innocent person.

response.rationale: The reply directly challenges the con responsibility revision with a framing case intended to show that deterrence and incapacitation omit a desert-sensitive moral distinction.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It squarely contacts the decisive replacement-rationale demand through a focused counterexample.

precisionFindings.rationale: The comparison between actual offender and framed innocent person is clear, stable, and expressly limited to forward-looking rationales.

calibrationFindings.rationale: As an objection showing insufficiency of deterrence alone, the framing comparison fits the asserted force.

charity.alternative: A forward-looking theory can independently prohibit framing through rights, institutional trust, and harmful-error constraints.
charity.decisiveQualification: Those constraints can distinguish the cases without establishing retributive desert.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The counterexample effectively challenges deterrence-only punishment, but does not entail a retributive conclusion by itself.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The thought experiment is well specified, though rival forward-looking explanations of its wrongness are not compared.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly attacks the con central responsibility-revision bridge at its justification of punishment.

representationalCharity.rationale: The objection targets deterrence alone and omits the strongest nonretributive rights-based response to framing.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt distinguishes abandoning retribution from retaining deterrence and introduces the innocent-framing example against that position.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Scientific causal explanations have repeatedly reduced blame and punishment while enabling more humane treatment rather than causing social collapse.
moves.attributionBasis: The response follows Huemer's explicit defense of retribution and uses a continuous historical series of causal reinterpretations attributed to Sapolsky.

components.text: Whether a nonretributive account can explain why framing an innocent person is wrong while restraining an actual offender is permissible.
Whether subtracting blame and retribution predictably causes social collapse or can support humane practice.

response.rationale: The historical examples substantively answer collapse concerns and support humane revision, but they do not contact the decisive innocent-framing distinction posed immediately beforehand.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: This is a relevant nonanswer to the primary framing objection, although it answers a secondary practical concern.

precisionFindings.rationale: The historical claim is clear, with the extrapolation from specific conditions to general responsibility revision left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The examples support humane causal reinterpretation, but not every proposed subtraction of responsibility or punishment.

charity.alternative: The framing objection concerns equal treatment of innocent and guilty persons, not fear that reduced blame causes social collapse.
charity.decisiveQualification: Historical humane reform does not supply the missing moral distinction between the framed innocent and actual offender.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The historical induction is coherent on its own terms, though it does not resolve the targeted desert objection.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Epilepsy, schizophrenia, and learning cases provide concrete support, with broad extrapolation remaining underdefended.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports humane responsibility revision despite failing to answer the selected framing objection.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply shifts to a weaker practical concern and omits the strongest, immediately preceding framing challenge.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites repeated reductions in blame after causal reinterpretation and claims these changes produced more humane treatment without collapse.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: No neural action has been shown independent of hormones, genes, development, and environment, so expanding causal knowledge warrants caution about blame and deserved advantage.
moves.attributionBasis: Sapolsky answers Huemer's skeptical-induction objection, issues the neuron-independence challenge, and carries its ethical implications through the end of his turn.

components.text: Whether the causal evidence shows only influence or instead justifies demanding an action independent of antecedent biological and environmental conditions.
Whether experienced freedom retains default authority as mechanistic causal knowledge expands.

response.rationale: The reply directly raises an independence challenge against the influence-only distinction and links expanding causal explanation to reduced confidence in blame, though absence of independence is not identical to determinism.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the decisive evidential challenge, with one important conceptual bridge still compressed.

precisionFindings.rationale: The neural-independence challenge is clear, but independence from influence can be stronger than the control thesis actually requires.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The absence of demonstrated independence warrants caution, while it does not alone prove exhaustive causal determination.

charity.alternative: Libertarian control need not require a neuron wholly independent of hormones, genes, development, or environment.
charity.decisiveQualification: Causal influence can coexist with control unless the influences are shown to exhaustively determine selection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The argument coherently motivates caution but risks conflating nonindependence from influences with absence of agent control.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The mechanistic factors are specific, but the universal no-independent-action conclusion lacks direct representative verification.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con central evidence bridge through a concrete mechanistic independence challenge.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply sets a demanding independence test and insufficiently addresses the strongest influence-with-control alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt asks for a neuron acting independently of hormones, food, genes, developmental adversity, and environmentally formed connections.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Without decisive scientific evidence for either determinism or freedom, the rational default is to accept the appearance that one has free will unless compelling contrary evidence emerges.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer explicitly turns to the larger scientific question and states a continuous epistemic argument from possible testing to the default of appearances.

components.text: Whether incomplete scientific evidence should displace the prima facie appearance that one possesses free will.
Whether historical failures of intuition defeat the default epistemic status of present appearances.

response.rationale: The reply directly answers the evidential challenge with a default rule favoring appearances absent compelling contrary evidence, although the reliability and burden allocation of that rule remain contested.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It clearly contacts the primary evidential demand and supplies an explicit competing burden rule.

precisionFindings.rationale: The default rule and defeater condition are explicit, but “everything” initially gives the rule an overly broad scope.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Acknowledged scientific inconclusiveness supports provisional belief, though not the unrestricted reliability of appearances.

charity.alternative: Some appearances may lack default authority when a specific error mechanism or strong skeptical induction is available.
charity.decisiveQualification: The con side still must connect its general causal evidence to a defeater for this particular appearance.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The defeasible-default structure is coherent, though the broad everything-appears rule needs a reliability qualification.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The move establishes an epistemic policy more than empirical reliability and does not compare alternative default rules.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the pro central epistemic bridge by allocating the burden against experienced freedom.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move allows compelling evidence to defeat appearances and thus fairly preserves the strongest qualified skeptical alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt states that free will seems present and should be accepted provisionally unless compelling contrary evidence appears.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: Scientific explanation does not require determinism because scientific theories may be indeterministic and an agent's reasons may explain behavior without determining it.
moves.attributionBasis: Huemer takes the floor after the audience question and gives a compact continuous answer citing quantum mechanics and reason-based explanation.

components.text: Whether scientific explanation requires deterministic causal closure rather than allowing indeterministic or reason-giving explanations.
Whether a complete explanation must exclude agent reasons that explain without determining the action.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the explanatory demand by separating scientific explanation from determinism and proposing reasons as nondetermining explanations, but it does not establish that such reasons provide libertarian control.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It is a partial answer reaching the decisive explanation-versus-determination component while leaving control unresolved.

precisionFindings.rationale: Indeterministic theory and nondetermining reason explanation are distinguishable, with their connection to agency left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: Quantum theory and reason explanation adequately establish the limited possibility that explanation need not entail determination.

charity.alternative: Indeterministic scientific theories show nondeterminism but do not show that choices are controlled rather than random.
charity.decisiveQualification: The move establishes conceptual compatibility, not the actuality or agency of indeterministic choice.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The compatibility argument is clear, with one bounded bridge from reason explanation to libertarian agency omitted.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Quantum mechanics supports indeterministic science, while the reason-giving example remains largely asserted.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It strongly supports the pro subsidiary explanation bridge by separating explanation from determination.

representationalCharity.rationale: The limited conclusion fairly preserves the opposing distinction between indeterminacy and agent control.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt cites quantum mechanics as scientific yet indeterministic and says behavior can be explained by citing an agent’s reasons.

moves.speaker: Michael Huemer
moves.proposition: An agent's reasons can explain a free choice even if there is no further explanation of why the agent selected those reasons over competing reasons.
moves.attributionBasis: The turn follows Huemer's earlier answer and develops his characteristic reasons-based account of libertarian choice.

components.text: Whether a choice can be intelligibly explained without tracing the final selection to a further determining antecedent.

response.rationale: The reply contacts the explanatory challenge by locating explanation in the agent’s reasons while conceding that explanation may terminate before explaining selection among competing reasons.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It directly addresses explanation but only partially answers why this reason rather than a competing reason controlled selection.

precisionFindings.rationale: The distinction between explaining action by a reason and explaining selection among reasons is expressly acknowledged.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The speaker’s explicit uncertainty accurately matches the limited claim that reasons can provide some explanation.

charity.alternative: If nothing explains why one reason prevailed, the residual selection may be random rather than controlled.
charity.decisiveQualification: Lack of further explanation does not itself establish either randomness or agent control.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The account distinguishes partial explanation from ultimate selection, but leaves the central agency bridge unresolved.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: Reason explanation is plausible but asserted without a developed account of how it controls an undetermined selection.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly addresses the pro subsidiary explanation bridge at the precise explanatory stopping point.

representationalCharity.rationale: The move candidly preserves the explanatory stopping-point problem but does not fully resolve its control implication.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt says a reason can explain the choice but concedes no further explanation for acting on it rather than competing reasons.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: A decision never becomes an unexplained act of agent selection because prior causes remain operative, and quantum indeterminacy does not supply agency.
moves.attributionBasis: The explicit contrast with the preceding view and the deterministic causal argument identify Sapolsky as the responding speaker.

components.text: Whether explanation legitimately stops at an agent’s reasons or prior causes remain operative through the final selection.
Whether quantum indeterminacy can supply the agency missing from a nondetermined choice.

response.rationale: The reply directly denies an unexplained stopping point and rejects quantum indeterminacy as a source of agency, contacting both decisive components but offering compressed warrants for each.

responsivenessWithinClass.rationale: It explicitly contacts the stopping-point and indeterminacy demands, though the substantive demonstrations are brief.

precisionFindings.rationale: Prior causation and quantum indeterminacy are clearly distinguished, with the universal causal scope left implicit.

calibrationFindings.rationale: The categorical claim that prior causes always exhaust the choice is asserted more strongly than the supplied argument supports.

charity.alternative: Reasons can explain an agent-controlled selection without determining it, and libertarian agency need not rest on quantum randomness.
charity.decisiveQualification: Rejecting randomness does not establish that prior causes exhaustively determine selection.

logicalCoherence.rationale: The response identifies the relevant dilemma but largely asserts continuous prior causation rather than demonstrating it.

evidenceWarrant.rationale: The universal causal claim and dismissal of quantum relevance receive little specific support in the excerpt.

relevanceBurden.rationale: It directly supports the con subsidiary indeterminacy bridge by separating randomness from authored control.

representationalCharity.rationale: The reply addresses indeterminacy but insufficiently distinguishes the strongest agent-causal or reasons-responsive alternative.

moves.evidenceBasis: The excerpt repeatedly invokes what happened before and then denies that microscopic quantum indeterminacy supplies free will.

moves.speaker: Robert Sapolsky
moves.proposition: Known biological and environmental causes leave no room for philosophically significant free will, including attempts to preserve it through compatibilism.
moves.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly addresses Sapolsky, whose answer identifies himself with an unusually uncompromising hard-incompatibilist position.

components.text: Whether nondetermining reason explanations can preserve a philosophically significant form of controlled choice.
Whether any account of free will survives known biological and environmental influences.

response.rationale: The reply categorically excludes all philosophical accounts by appeal to known causes, but it does not analyze the decisive nondetermining-reasons proposal or any particular compatibilist control criterion.
